title: Cardiorenal Interactions in Transcatheter Structural Heart Interventions: Mechanisms, Renal Outcomes, and Clinical Implications
content: A Structural heart interventions are being performed more routinely in patients with severe valvular heart disease who are at high surgical risk. Because many of these patients have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and multiple comorbidities, the stability of renal function has become an important component of procedural success. This review summarizes the current evidence on renal outcomes following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER), tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) and transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR). We reviewed clinical trials, registries, observational studies and meta-analyses evaluating acute kidney injury, renal recovery, and long-term kidney outcomes after these procedures. Studies shows that although AKI remains associated with increased mortality and adverse clinical outcomes, kidney function remains stable or improves in many patients after successful valve intervention. Improvement appears to be most evident in patients with reversible hemodynamic impairment or venous congestion, particularly following tricuspid interventions. Current studies also suggest that changes in renal function after intervention may provide additional information beyond baseline kidney function. Future studies should adopt standardized renal endpoints and further evaluate factors associated with renal recovery to improve patient selection and long-term outcomes.
